::: {.pub-title}
Quantifying drought-induced systemic risk in the Polish economy through an integrated Nature Value-at-Risk and Dynamic Inoperability Input–Output approach
:::

::: {.pub-meta}
Gacek, K., & Santos, J. R. — *Risk Analysis* · IF 3.3 [under review]{.pub-status}
:::

<details class="abstract">
<summary>Abstract</summary>
<div class="abstract-body">
<p>An integrated framework that couples a Nature Value-at-Risk perspective with Dynamic
Inoperability Input–Output modelling to quantify the systemic economic risk generated by
drought in Poland, including the cumulative losses accumulated along the recovery path.</p>
</div>

## Peer-reviewed articles

::: {.pub}
[2026]{.pub-year}

::: {.pub-title}
Who pulls, who pushes? Mapping Poland's 2020 water footprint and key sectors via Input–Output backward/forward linkages
:::

::: {.pub-meta}
Gacek, K. — *Water Resources and Industry*, 35, 100368 · IF 7.5 · [doi.org/10.1016/j.wri.2026.100368](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.wri.2026.100368)
:::

<details class="abstract">
<summary>Abstract</summary>
<div class="abstract-body">
<p>The study maps how water use propagates through Poland's economy, joining the 2020 national
Input–Output accounts with sectoral withdrawal data from Statistics Poland in a consistent
environmentally extended framework. Direct and indirect water use is derived from the Leontief
model, and three complementary pairs of linkages — total, size-adjusted and net, each with a
backward and a forward component — classify every sector as key, backward-oriented,
forward-oriented or weak.</p>
<p>Withdrawals prove extremely concentrated: electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning,
chemicals, and paper together account for 94.2% of industrial withdrawals, while 65.3% of
economy-wide water use arises indirectly, upstream of the sector that meets final demand. Direct
effects dominate in 32 sectors and indirect effects in 27. The linkage measures expose systemic
roles that headline withdrawal figures hide — food and beverage service activities show strong
size-adjusted backward reach, and architectural and engineering services very high linkages in
both directions — while 62 of 77 sectors fall into the weak category.</p>
<p>The contribution is threefold: an economy-wide decomposition that combines linkages with
concentration metrics to locate policy leverage points; a size-adjusted indicator set that
separates scale from systemic reach and so permits fair comparison across sectors; and a
majority-rule classification that turns six linkage measures into a practical basis for choosing
between supplier-focused, buyer-standards-based and dual interventions. Water-intensive
industries, the study concludes, need to move from isolated facility-level efficiency to
management of the whole value chain.</p>
</div>
</details>

::: {.pub}
[2025]{.pub-year}

::: {.pub-title}
Industrial waste in Poland (2010–2020): a sectoral view using Input–Output models and structural decomposition analysis
:::

::: {.pub-meta}
Gacek, K. — *Acta Universitatis Lodziensis. Folia Oeconomica*, 1–24 · [doi.org/10.18778/0208-6018.371.01](https://doi.org/10.18778/0208-6018.371.01)
:::

<details class="abstract">
<summary>Abstract</summary>
<div class="abstract-body">
<p>The paper traces industrial waste generation in the Polish economy over the decade 2010–2020,
asking how technological change and shifts in final demand jointly shaped the volume and
composition of waste. Environmentally extended Input–Output models are combined with structural
decomposition analysis: using Polish Input–Output tables for 2010 and 2020 together with waste
data aggregated into 17 sectoral clusters, the change in waste output is decomposed into waste
intensity, technology and final demand components, with further disaggregation into product-mix
adjustments, demand composition and sector-specific technological change. Final demand emerges as
the dominant driver of the increase. Technological change works in both directions — the largest
reduction appears in electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply, while waste collection,
treatment and disposal together with materials recovery records a marked increase — and mining
and quarrying as well as construction play key roles.</p>
</div>
</details>

::: {.tags}
- Input–Output Models
- Waste Generation
- Leontief Models
- Structural Decomposition Analysis
:::
:::

::: {.pub}
[2025]{.pub-year}

::: {.pub-title}
Sectoral interdependencies and waste generation in Poland (2010–2018): insights from Input–Output analysis
:::

::: {.pub-meta}
Gacek, K. — *Economics and Environment*, 92(1), 798 · IF 1.0 · [doi.org/10.34659/eis.2025.92.1.798](https://doi.org/10.34659/eis.2025.92.1.798)
:::

<details class="abstract">
<summary>Abstract</summary>
<div class="abstract-body">
<p>The study investigates the interdependencies between economic activity and waste generation in
the Polish economy, identifying key sectors and tracking how their classification changed between
2010 and 2018. Five pairs of backward and forward linkages are computed from Input–Output tables.
Mining and quarrying, manufacturing and energy emerge as the primary contributors. Taking sector
size into account makes it possible to compare parts of the economy that differ in function and
scale, and on that basis agriculture, forestry and fishing together with two manufacturing
sectors also qualify as key sectors. The paper documents shifts in the waste profile of sectors
and supplies an empirical base for targeted policy interventions.</p>
</div>
</details>

::: {.pub}
[2024]{.pub-year}

::: {.pub-title}
Tracing the drivers of waste generation in Poland (2010–2018): a structural decomposition and Input–Output approach
:::

::: {.pub-meta}
Gacek, K. — *Bulletin of Geography. Socio-Economic Series*, 63, 75–85 · IF 0.8 · [doi.org/10.12775/bgss-2024-0006](https://doi.org/10.12775/bgss-2024-0006)
:::

<details class="abstract">
<summary>Abstract</summary>
<div class="abstract-body">
<p>The paper applies structural decomposition analysis within an extended Input–Output model to
trace the main sources of waste generation in Poland between 2010 and 2018. Economic growth over
that period was accompanied by rising waste volumes, with the quantities produced depending on
sectoral output and on a number of underlying factors. The decomposition shows how changes in
final demand and in technology affected the waste generated by individual sectors over the
period analysed, and the paper argues that the technique is a valuable tool for environmental
analysis, giving a comprehensive view of the links between economic activity, environmental
impact and waste generation.</p>
</div>
</details>
